Section 1
Jeremy Hunt, the UK's Health Secretary, found himself in an unusual and highly public dispute that began not in the halls of Parliament, but on social media. The confrontation started after Hunt appeared on The Andrew Marr Show, where he boldly claimed that the NHS had overseen "the biggest expansion of mental health provision in Europe." This statement, made with confidence on national television, would soon come back to haunt him in ways he likely never anticipated. What followed was one of the most unusual political spats in recent memory, playing out not through official channels but through the very public forum of Twitter.

Section 2
The challenge to Hunt's claims came from an unexpected source: Ralf Little, a comedy actor best known for playing Anthony in the beloved British sitcom The Royle Family. Little, clearly passionate about the state of mental healthcare in the UK, publicly accused Hunt of "knowingly lying" to the public about NHS mental health statistics. In a bold move, Little told the Health Secretary to sue him if he was wrong, effectively throwing down the gauntlet and daring Hunt to defend his claims. This was no small accusation, and it quickly drew widespread public attention.

Section 3
The controversy surrounding Hunt's mental health statistics was not an isolated incident. Just a month prior, Hunt had been forced to row back on a claim made to Parliament that the NHS had seen an increase of 30,000 mental health workers - a figure that turned out to be 43 times higher than the actual number. Despite this recent embarrassment, Hunt chose to engage directly with Little's challenge. A week after Little's initial accusation, the Health Secretary responded with a string of statistics and boldly "double dared" Little to prove otherwise, escalating what could have been a minor social media spat into a full-blown public debate.

Section 4
Little rose to the challenge in spectacular fashion, posting a thread of more than 40 tweets methodically rebutting each of Hunt's claims. The actor backed his arguments with statistics from Full Fact, an independent UK fact-checking charity, lending credibility and weight to his counter-arguments. The thread quickly went viral, being shared more than 15,000 times, demonstrating just how deeply the public cared about the state of mental healthcare in the UK. Far from being dismissed as a celebrity stunt, Little's detailed and well-researched rebuttal earned widespread respect and kept the pressure firmly on the Health Secretary.

Section 5
Rather than backing down, Hunt doubled down further, responding with an extraordinary series of 26 tweets of his own, though the thread became difficult to follow after he lost the chronological order midway through. Hunt cited training programs, including 8,000 mental health nurses currently in training and a 25% increase in nurse training places, as evidence of the government's commitment to mental healthcare. However, his credibility took another hit when it emerged that he had quoted from a New York Times article that had been corrected three times, following challenges from former shadow minister for mental health Luciana Berger. The ongoing Twitter battle highlighted not only the fractious state of NHS mental health provision but also the growing power of social media to hold even the most senior politicians publicly accountable.
